utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The examination-in-chief of the accused continues.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I would like to inform the technical booth that we have a problem with our notebooks here. We don't have a transcript on the screens. So if we can get some assistance, I would be grateful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps something will be done. Is it both the screen and the laptop?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Probably it's an issue of the programme or arrangements with the -- with the LiveNote transcript on laptops, yeah, notebooks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The screen is okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The screen is okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We can move along, and then in the meantime I hope that some of our friends from the technical unit will resolve the issue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, doctor. Tell me, yesterday we were discussing the activities of the Crisis Staff in the second half of April 1992, and now in order to make this as systematic as possible, I would like to move in chronological order month by month. I would be interested in the following: What can you tell us about the period, say, a few weeks before mid-April and the course of the month of April itself? Were there any liquidations of SDS officials in the area? Were there any provocations and various incidents around Samac in the region of Odzak? What can you tell us about this? Generally speaking, what was the situation like from that point of view?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I already said that the situation was very tense, that the programme of the Croatian Community of Bosanska Posavina was being implemented in all municipalities, and that the only municipality where the job had not been completed yet was Bosanski Samac. Political officials of the Serb Democratic Party were eliminated practically in all of these municipalities. The president of the municipal board of the SDS, Milovan Milosevic, was killed in Derventa. Then the president of the municipal board of the SDS in Bosanski Brod was killed as well, Miroslav Radovanovic. Then the president of the municipal board of the SDS Odzak, Dragomir Tesanovic, was arrested, and he was subjected to unseen torture. Then the president of the municipal board of the SDS, Stevo Josipovic, was expelled from Orasje. And finally, they made an effort to get me here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, do you know any official of the SDS who had a nickname Trumam? What happened to him?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Truman was president of the local SDS community in Donja Dubica in the territory of Odzak and he was killed on the 18th or 19th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Excuse me. Sorry to interrupt. The Bench will also require the same -- similar assistance for the laptops.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: This man nicknamed Truman, what was his first and last name?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: His name is Rajko, Rajko Djuric.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Where was Rajko Djuric killed?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: He was killed in the village of Prud [Realtime transcript read in error "Brod"], municipality of Samac, on the other side of the Bosna, on the other side of the Bosna River.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just a correction to the transcript. Page 3, line 12, instead of "village of Brod," it should be "village of Prud", P-r-u-d. Could we have -- Mr. Usher -- could we have -- Ms. Usher, sorry, your assistance. P9A.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you explain to us, doctor, what Prud actually is. Is it part of the Samac municipality? How far away is it? Can you give us a bit more detail?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: It is part of the Samac municipality, but at that time -- I mean, it's on the other side of the Bosna River. So right by the town of Samac but the River Bosna separates the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could you please show Prud to us.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: This is Samac, and this is Prud [Realtime transcript read in error "Brod"].

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Again, correction in the transcript. It's not "Brod," it's Prud. Ms. Usher, thank you very much for your assistance. You may take your seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So Prud is an integral part of the municipality of Samac? It's one of the local communes of Samac?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What is your personal knowledge about the period just before the armed conflict broke out in Samac with regard to the activities of some of the helmsmen of the SDA and the HDZ from Samac as well as members of the TO and certain paramilitary formations? Were there any contacts between them? Where did these contacts take place? Where did these meetings take place? What was discussed and what was the influence of these activities on the atmosphere in Samac? What you know, of course.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Could you put a shorter question, a more accurate question, a more precise question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you know something about contacts between the helmsmen of the SDA and the HDZ just before the war conflict broke out in Samac? Do you know about any meetings between them? Do you know about their plans? Do you know about the establishment of some of their joint organs, or do you know nothing?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Information was coming in that they had formed military units, that they had armed themselves, that they had set up a Crisis Staff in Prud, that they have an operative plan to take over Samac. Then the information was coming in that Muslims had established all of that on their own as well, that is to say, together with the Croats on the one hand, and on the other hand only the Muslims. So there would be an exclusively Muslim command, an exclusively Muslim staff, Crisis Staff, and that they brought in a lot of weapons, explosives, mines, and that they created plans to take over the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you have a specific name that is mentioned in relation to these activities?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: In relation to these activities, Sulejman Tihic is invariably mentioned, as well as Alija Fitozovic; Mate Nujic; Filipovic; Marko Bozanovic; the chief of police, Dragan Lukac, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: At that time, what position did Sulejman Tihic hold?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Sulejman Tihic was an assemblyman in the municipal assembly and he was president of the municipal board of the Party of Democratic Action in Samac and a member of the top leadership of the SDA at the level of all of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Who was Alija Fitozovic?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Alija Fitozovic, according to what people were saying then, was commander of the military wing of the Party of Democratic Action in Samac. He was a member of the executive board of the Party of the Democratic Action, and later he was appointed Chief of Staff of their Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What party did Mato Nujic come from?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Mato Nujic was from the Croat Democratic Union.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What about Marko Bozanovic?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: The HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What is the role of Dragan Lukac in all of this?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Dragan Lukac took over the police, so he carried out his job. What other jobs he had to do, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: On whose behalf did he take over the police?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: On behalf of the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me. I just have a question, Dr. Simic, with respect to the last answer. Does the -- or did, rather, the chief of police in Bosanski Samac usually act in that position on behalf of a political party? Because in response to your question on whose behalf did he take over the police, your answer is, "On behalf of the HDZ." And I'm just wondering, is -- was that usual up to and, say, before the armed conflict broke out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is one of the remains of the Communist system. The chief of police was considered to be a political appointee. Before one party, the League of Communists, would delegate its own chief of police. However, after the first democratic elections, the three parties decided who would be chief of police, or they would put forward a proposal to the minister who to appoint. So we had an inter-party agreement that all three parties would have a joint proposal for chief of police, and that was Vinko Dragicevic, that is to say that without the agreement of all three parties, the chief of police could not change. But this was done overnight without the consent of the Serb side and Dragan Lukac took over the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Who appointed Dragan Lukac chief of staff?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. However, the Serb side did not take part in this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I apologise for the interruption of my colleague, but here we have a question. It's page 7, line 1: Who appointed Dragan Lukac Chief of Staff? And this would probably cause some misunderstanding, because he was not in the staff of TO or whatever. He was the chief of the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for the correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So let's repeat this question for the transcript. Who appointed Dragan Lukac chief of police in Bosanski Samac? What was the competent authority for that kind of thing?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that, but the Serb side did not take part in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. This is only for the transcript. Tell me, Dr. Simic, at the beginning of May, do you have any knowledge regarding the killing of some Serb soldiers at Grebnice? What happened at the beginning of May? Do you have any knowledge regarding this?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: There were killings every day. I need a precise question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: During the first ten days of May, do you remember -- well, I'm not going to say mass killing, but certainly, say, 10 or 15 persons were wounded on a bus.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was in Novo Selo, this bus of soldiers of the Army of Republika Srpska was bullet-riddled from an ambush.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When did this occur? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: The first half of May. I think it was by the 10th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge about the killing of non-Serb population by Lugar in Crkvina?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, regrettably. We learned about that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Also around the 10th of May. I don't know the exact day, but it was around those days.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge with regard to the fact that this incident in which Lugar took part, whether it took place before or after this event when in Novo Selo on the bus Serb soldiers were wounded and killed?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I think that this happened afterwards, after the massacre on this bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What was your personal reaction when you heard about the killings in Crkvina committed by Lugar?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I think it was condemned by all citizens of Samac municipality as a dishonourable and ruthless act, and this has brought shame on us until the present day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Please tell me, was something done officially after that incident?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: We asked all competent authorities, especially the judiciary, to process that, to bring them to trial, to try them, and to punish them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And what were the competent judicial organs at the time?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: At the time there already started emerging a small vacuum in the judiciary. There was no military judiciary because the Yugoslav People's Army was withdrawing and taking its military courts with it, and the Army of Republika Srpska was only in the process of being established and was only setting up its military courts, and it wasn't done until the 6th of June of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Dr. Simic, what do you know about the incidents and imprisonment of a large number of Serbs in Odzak -- in the Odzak area, rather? When did this take place? Who was involved in it? How many Serbs were involved? And then later on, I will put a few more questions regarding this.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: This is something that will be discussed at greater length by one of the co-accused. The information we received was that Serb residents of Odzak were imprisoned, that they were all put into camps, and that the process of liquidation, extinction, rape, torture, and looting of the entire property had commenced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I'm having some problems with the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: If my mic is switched on, then you cannot --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Oh, that's the problem. Dr. Simic, I just have a question. Just going back to the questions by Mr. Pantelic concerning Lugar and the competent judicial authorities. I don't really see an answer in the sense that you said that you asked all competent authorities to process that, but then your subsequent answer, you said there was a vacuum in the judiciary and also that military courts in Republika Srpska were not set up until the 6th of June, 1992. So my question is: So what happened with Lugar? Did nothing happen, because there was a vacuum in the civil -- civilian criminal courts? Or when the military courts were set up on the 6th of June, 1992, was something done to activate a military court investigation at that time? Because, of course, we've heard from many of the witnesses that there were military courts, I believe, in Brcko I think, so if you could just help with that, I think it would be of assistance, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the 10th until the 20th of May, the Yugoslav People's Army withdrew. Those who were not from Bosnia withdrew beyond the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And by doing so, the military courts of the Yugoslav People's Army were withdrawn as well. I am aware of it now that there was a vacuum in the judiciary; however, then we did not know about that. We expected the Yugoslav People's Army, who had a direct command over those volunteers -- we expected the army to arrest them and to try them. However, they were withdrawing and they did not do that. Lugar was later arrested and expelled. And then once again when he came back in the fall or during wintertime, he was then arrested and tried in Banja Luka. There was another trial at the high military court in Han Pijesak, but I don't think this case was in fact ever brought to an end by military authorities. I think that they looked into it but didn't, in fact, ever put him to trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, let us go back to the events in Odzak. Based on your information, when were the Serbs imprisoned in Odzak? When did all of this take place?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: All of that was taking place at the beginning of May, and my co-accused will give you specific information. I don't know the exact dates, and I wouldn't like to give you erroneous information now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well, Dr. Simic. You can tell me -- if you don't remember, you can tell me so or you can just give me an approximate date. What was the reaction of the Samac population regarding that? Did they have any relatives in Odzak that were imprisoned? What was the reaction in town among the residents when this took place in Odzak at the beginning of May, as you said? What do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, their reaction was fierce. Since this is an area that is quite close to our town, 2 to 5 kilometres away as the crow flies, and people have many relatives in both places. Some families had some members living on one side and the other members of that family lived on the other side, and some of them left the area before the war but still a lot of families were divided between these two places, so members of families started coming in from other areas, from abroad as well, looking for their family members and asking that something be done to help those who had been imprisoned. 24

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you know - did you know then or have you learned later on - how many Serbs were imprisoned in Odzak then, approximately?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: The information that we received was that 4.000 Serbs had been imprisoned of all ages, from babies to the elderly, women and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you once again to speak slower and to wait at least five seconds before answering my question; otherwise, the transcript will not be accurate. What was the reaction in the Crisis Staff? Did you discuss the situation about the imprisoned Serbs? Did you go to somebody asking for assistance as the Crisis Staff? What did you as an institution do regarding this issue of Serbs imprisoned in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: The pressure of the families was quite intense. We talked about that almost on a daily basis. But the only thing that we could do was to write letters and send it to all addresses that we were aware of and ask for help. And about every few days, we would send out letters to various organs in Yugoslavia, to the leadership of the Serb Orthodox Church, asking them to appeal to the international organisations, asking for assistance, and asking them to enable these people to leave the area. In fact, their only request was to be enabled to leave the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, did any of your fellow citizens of Serb ethnicity offer to be a go-between on a voluntary basis in negotiations with Croats about imprisoned Serbs? Did the Crisis Staff coordinate something regarding this? Were any contacts established? What do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: All of the people who hailed from that municipality, from that side of the Bosna River, felt responsible, felt it was their duty to help these people in despair. One of the eldest among them was Miroslav Tadic, and he established first contacts through the centre for information, from the Ministry of Defence, he established contacts with the Odzak side, and this is how the negotiations started between the Odzak and the Samac side.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Was a number of non-Serbs at that time detained at the stadium in Crkvina?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. We received information that a small number of civilians of Croat ethnicity was imprisoned in the culture hall in Crkvina, and then soon thereafter we also received information that all of them had been sent home with apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Pantelic, just for clarification, your question on page 13, line 1, was: Were they detained in the stadium in Crkvina? Dr. Simic's answer is that they were imprisoned in the culture hall in Crkvina. I know from some of the witnesses we heard about the stadium. I don't recall about the culture hall. I remember a gymnasium and -- rather, a stadium and adjoining building but not a culture hall. So it might be the translation or not. Maybe you could just clarify the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, Your Honour, I will do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You heard what Her Honour Williams said. Some witnesses mentioned a stadium in Crkvina, and now we -- please let me finish. Let's clarify this. And another matter, doctor: Please watch the screen in front of you. And when the cursor stops, then you can start answering, because it is in your interest that everything you say is properly recorded. I fully understand you. You want to reveal your account of the events. You've waited for this for a long time. But I have to tell you that we cannot properly do our job if we do not have an accurate transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: The culture hall in Crkvina and the sport fields, the stadium, are right next to each other. The culture hall is the covered area, and the stadium is an outdoor field, but they're right next to each other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you. So we are talking, then, about the same thing. Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Just a matter that concerns the Prosecution. Mr. Pantelic asked Dr. Simic of details of the first contacts with the people in Odzak, and that was done through Mr. Tadic. And that was how negotiations started. His next question is this: Was there -- were there a number of non-Serbs detained at the stadium in Crkvina? And the witness gave his answer. It's not apparent to me if those two matters are connected, and I don't know if that's what Mr. Pantelic is trying to establish. But if he is trying to establish, then it should be made clear. In other words, is what happened in Crkvina somehow related to the negotiations regarding the exchange for the Serbs in Odzak, or are we moving on to a completely different and unrelated topic? Because if it is related, then the witness ought to be given his opportunity to say so and we ought to be clear about it. If it's unrelated, fine, and we can move on to this completely new topic. But as it arose at that point in time, I would like to know is the witness's position that the round-up of Croats at Crkvina was a reaction to the detention of Serbs in Odzak or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic. I'm sure the request by the Prosecution is clear. And can we have clarification from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Your Honour. Well, I would not say that I'm -- that my intention is to make some kind of fling between -- I'm just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no, no. Just ask -- the witness understood the Prosecution's intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Ask the witness to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour. But maybe that's a matter for clarification in cross-examination of my learned friend. I will do that rather now. It's no problem. But it's not my job to make any assumptions or connection with that regard. What I'm doing, Your Honour, is to put certain episodes during the time period, time frame, and that's my job. But of course I will clarify it -- I will clarify that with Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The Prosecution, if they misunderstand anything, they're entitled to ask for clarification from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, in cross-examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no, no. Even when --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: According to the Rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no, no. Even when you're examination-in-chiefing, there are certain rurals that the --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can you go ahead to ask the accused to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Because this is a matter of legal issue, Your Honour. I'm speaking about factual matters here, but I will clarify it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I will clarify that. Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Just go ahead and do your job and listen to what the Trial Chamber says.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I will do my job according to your -- legal standards, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Oh, that your view that you won't take the instructions of the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I am taking your instructions, and I will immediately ask my client about all these things. Of course.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel also pause between question and answer, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The detention of the civilians in Crkvina, did it have anything to do with Odzak?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Who detained non-Serb civilians at the stadium in Crkvina?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: How long were non-Serb civilians from Samac detained in Crkvina?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Stevan Todorovic reported that it was for one afternoon only.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Who did he report to?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: In May, in May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Who organised the transport of these people from Crkvina to Samac?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did Stevan Todorovic report again to the Crisis Staff about this sometime after mid-May?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, in mid-May, since you mentioned it, the JNA pulled out from the area of Samac, did it? What do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, in mid-May all active-duty officers and other soldiers who were not from Bosnia-Herzegovina left the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, do you know who was the commander of the JNA units prior to the pullout of the JNA from Samac?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Colonel Stevan Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And after he left, do you know who took over the command over the practically newly set up army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Retired Colonel Mico Djurdjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And what was that unit called, that unit commanded by retired Colonel Djurdjevic?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: These are military issues, to which I do not know the answer, and I'll explain why.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I'm only asking you about the name of the unit, if you happen to know it, the number of the brigade. You don't have to answer if you don't know.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: At that moment I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Why didn't you know that at that moment?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't know it to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But did you learn it during this case or during these years following 1992 what that unit was called?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: When I read the documents for the Defence, I read that there were three laws at that time: A law which supported the Yugoslav People's Army, a law which supported the Territorial Defence, and the law on the establishment of the Army of Republika Srpska. At that time, all these three laws were there. Which one was in force? Which army? Was it the Yugoslav People's Army? Was the Territorial Defence? Was it the army of Republika Srpska? I did not know at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When did you meet retired Colonel Djurdjevic and on what occasion?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I met him on the 14th or the 15th of April at a meeting in the municipal hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, how long did Colonel Djurdjevic head that military unit?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: For about a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you have a hand in any personnel decisions? Did you personally or the Crisis Staff try to impose some personnel decisions regarding that office, that is, his replacement at the head of that unit?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And do you know who succeeded him as the commander?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: For a while it was Dragan Djordjevic, Crni, who assumed his post for a few months. And then Lieutenant Colonel Mile Beronja for three years until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And who was the immediate superior of that military unit in Samac commanded by Colonel Djurdjevic?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Colonel Djurdjevic's superior was Colonel Dencic, who was still a member of the Tuzla Corps, that is, the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you communicate with Colonel Dencic?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, once.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And when was that and on what occasion?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: It was -- it had to do with the visit in Ugljevik and the pressure by the army to -- that Colonel Djurdjevic, because of his advanced age, was no longer able to command the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And that was when approximately?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I think it was the period of the beginning of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And what was the decision -- or rather, what was the role -- what was the role of the Crisis Staff, that is, your role in attending this meeting with Colonel Dencic?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: The role of the Crisis Staff was non-existent.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You mean it was exclusively a military matter concerning the appointments and personnel decisions? Is that what you are telling us?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, in May Mr. Milan Simic was appointed the president of the municipality of Samac. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just a correction to the transcript, page 19, line 19. It is not the position of president of the municipality. It's a position of the president of the executive board of the municipality of Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the Crisis Staff appointed Milan Simic, an economist, as the president of the executive board of the municipal assembly. And who ran against him in these elections?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Mirko Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Will you explain to us how was it decided, how did this decision come about to elect Mr. Simic the president of the executive council? Who was it that in a way lobbied for Mr. Simic and who nominated Mr. Lukic? What were their qualifications? Will you please give us some views about that episode.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: My proposal was to appoint Mirko Lukic as the president of the executive council because that post had been vacated. However, Stevan Todorovic nominated Milan Simic, managed to win over several members of the Crisis Staff. And when it came to voting, Milan Simic won.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So, if I may put it that way, you ask your option were outvoted in the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did Milan Simic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me. In terms of the voting on the Crisis Staff, how did it -- how did it work, Dr. Simic? Was it -- did every member have an equal vote, one vote? And the nominations, did they have to come from members of the Crisis Staff or could they come from outside persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The nominations always came from the executive council. And when it came to personnel appointments, then councilmen also had the right to nominate individual people -- I mean, councilmen in the municipal assembly. But it also went through the executive council and was put to vote at the municipal assembly or at that time, but only for a short period of time, by the Crisis Staff. We had the one-man-one-vote principle, and for a decision to become final, it had to be a majority of more than one half of members voting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Just one follow-up question: You told us yesterday that Mr. Stevan Todorovic, albeit that he was chief of police, was not a member of the Crisis Staff. So in what capacity -- what capacity did he have to nominate Milan Simic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As of the second assembly, he was on the roster of the members of the executive council, and therefore he was entitled to make his proposals at the executive council. And the executive body as the executive body always submits its proposal to the parliament. It is always the executive council which does it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And what do you know about some family or friendly relations between Stevan Todorovic and Milan Simic?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Milan Simic is Stevan Todorovic's in-law. He married his cousin, his first cousin. Before the war -- before the war, they were together, engaged in certain private business deals and were friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sometime in late autumn of 1992, did Milan Simic and Stevan Todorovic -- were Milan Simic and Stevan Todorovic arrested by military authorities?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Was it then that the corridor was closed by some volunteer units and military persons who were in close communication with Milan Simic and Stevan Todorovic?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: The corridor was closed for 12 to 18 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And who did that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Mostly the soldiers of the strike battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And in relation to this and some other incidents in military units, were there the proceedings conducted against them at the Banja Luka military court?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. All the responsible participants were arrested and brought before the court in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, for the purposes of clarification, the witness has referred to an organ called the strike battalion. There's been a lot of evidence in the case of a -- an organ consisting of paramilitaries. It might be of use for you to know if the strike battalion is the paramilitaries or some other -- some other body. And I know I can clarify it in cross-examination, but it's fair to the witness -- he's putting his story now, so you should have it clearly, so I submit it's a -- it's an inquiry that should be followed up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can we have clarification as sought by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Under whose command were the members of that strike battalion, as you call it?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Under the command of the officers of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, if you don't know, you don't have to tell us, but is that strike battalion the same thing as the special purpose battalion?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: It's one in the same battalion, but the terms are different.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Were they within the 2nd Posavina Brigade?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Who was commander of that brigade?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Commander of the 2nd Posavina Brigade was Lieutenant Colonel Mile Beronja.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So the 2nd Posavina Brigade is a unit of the Army of the Republika Srpska. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Milan Simic and Stevan Todorovic, were they freed -- or rather, were they released from military detention sometime late in the autumn of 1992 after these incidents that had to do with the battalion?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: My question was not properly interpreted, so I am going to repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... In fact, my question was related to the incidents with the blockage of the corridor, of the closing of the corridor, not -- not to the incidents within the battalion. So it's a rather different story. Just for the record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us go back to the month of June 1992. Sometime in the beginning of June you travelled to Belgrade, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could you explain who you went to see, who you travelled with from Samac. Could you give us a few details regarding that episode.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: The trip was of a humanitarian nature exclusively. Most of the civilian population of the municipality of Samac was in refugee camps in Serbia. The smaller part, belonging to -- I mean, all ethnic groups. The smaller part of the civilian population wanted to go to refugee camps in Serbia as well so that they would not be in the war zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting you, but among the refugees were there any Muslims and Croats who were in Serbia as well?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: All our wounded were staying in hospitals in Serbia, and they were in rehabilitation centres. All our gravely wounded persons who had paraplegia or quadriplegia were put up at various spas in Serbia. We were not in a position to pay for their stay there or for their treatment there. We could not even buy prosthetic devices for the disabled persons. We went to see Andjelko Maslic, our countryman, in order to ask for assistance. People given by persons coming from the -- assistance coming by persons coming from the same area. We wanted these people to stay in the refugee camps so that they would not be thrown out of refugee camps from rehabilitation centres, from hospitals, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. Why would they be thrown out of hospitals? Was it because there were no relations between social funds, or simply for some other reason? Why would people be thrown out of hospitals? Could you explain that, please.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: The reasons were the following: We could not pay. We could not pay for a single day of their treatment; however, they were never thrown out. The second reason was that the number of wounded persons was on the rise day after day from all parts of Republika Srpska. And the third reason why we left was the detention of Serbs, of the Serb population, in the territory of the municipality of Odzak, where again we wanted to convey some information and to try to appeal to have these people assisted through international organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Who was with you in this delegation, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Milos Bogdanovic. Miroslav Tadic, I, Stevan Todorovic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When you finished this meeting at Mr. Andjelko Maslic's, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Then Stevan Todorovic took us to have coffee with his best man, Colonel Jeremic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Where did this happen?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: This was at the premises of the Air Force, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did Stevan Todorovic mention something else to you in relation to that meeting? I mean, when you went to see his friend and best man. Did he mention any other reason except for going to have a cup of coffee?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Stevan Todorovic always attached importance to himself, but it was importance that he did not have. Then he tried to make up for this, with some other persons and some other connections.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting, Dr. Simic. When I said that you should speak slower, I didn't mean that slow. I mean, try to strike a balance between that fast manner of speech and what you're saying now so that you can hear in your headphones a flow of interpretation. Please. Because now it is too slow. I do apologise, but could you speak at a normal pace, like the way you talk.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: At that meeting, we stayed about 40 minutes; we talked about all our problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Who else was present at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: One or two other men were present, but I don't know who they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What was discussed specifically there? Who spoke the most and what was the topic tackled there? Were you surprised to have been there in the first place?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I was surprised. That was the first and the last time that I went to that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, these people who were with you at this meeting, did they also talk? Did they also take part in the discussion? Did they behave in a friendly way towards Stevan? After all, did you meet each other or were they already there at the time when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: They were already there when we arrived. We shook hands. Time went by quickly, and I do not recall all of the details of that conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When did you return to Samac?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: The same evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me the following: You said that your wife was heavily pregnant at the time.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Was it possible for you to visit her? Because she was about 50 kilometres away from Samac.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Because the army was between us, the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Dr. Simic, on page 24 -- in fact, page 23, line 25 and then the first couple of lines on page 24 Mr. Pantelic had asked you, in fact, two or three questions following one another. The first was: At that meeting, what was discussed specifically there? And then he went on and asked you whether you were surprised. And you answered that you were surprised but you didn't answer as to what was specifically discussed. I know you said you discussed your problems in an earlier answer, but you didn't respond to counsel's question as to the specifics. So if you can remember, you know, it might be useful.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said later that this was ten years ago and that -- as for the details of these 40 minutes of this discussion, I do not recall them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Usher, please, I have documents to tender into evidence. This is the medical list for -- Mira Simic, the wife of the witness, also the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Before we proceed, I just wanted to ask the accused that -- it's rather interesting to note that you remember exactly how long the meeting, the discussion took, that was 40 minutes, that was ten years ago. But you can't remember any of the details of the discussion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 40 minutes go by very quickly. In a war situation a municipality has so many problems that if every one of us took up a few minutes and spoke, that time would have gone by.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. -- I thought I -- Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. If you -- the Chamber has finished with its inquiries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: There's just one matter arising out of this exhibit that I'd like to raise briefly, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: It's this: Mr. Pantelic provided us with a folder of his documents which were categorised and placed under various - what's the word - headings or categories. It's like an index, in effect. For various reasons, analysis of the transcript, it's important for the Prosecution to know which section or -- it comes from so that we can later, when the time comes, analyse the transcript. I would be grateful if Mr. Pantelic could tell us which -- where it comes from in his folder that he provided to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. The internal number is R14.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Simic, please take a look at this document and tell us briefly what this is about.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: This is the fourth childbirth of my wife, Caesarean section, at the maternity ward in Doboj, on the 20th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your daughter was born then. What's her name?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Aleksandra.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You did not manage to visit your newborn daughter and your wife after she delivered the baby?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: During those first few days, it was not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Was Samac surrounded?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: By which military forces?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Seven brigades of the HVO, a brigade of the Muslim army, and the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Since you did your residency in Doboj for a while, in the lower right-hand corner, who is this doctor? Did you perhaps know him?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I did not. This is Dr. Hasandic. He is a Muslim by ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: If there is any objections, Your Honour, I would like to tender this document into exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have the numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It will be D59/1 ter and D59/1. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Mr. Pantelic, I believed or at least we have it on the transcript, on line 16, that you asked Dr. Simic did he -- did he know the doctor in the right-hand corner, and that would be Dr. Spasojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In fact, my question was to the left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: It says to the right in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yeah. That's maybe my mistake. I will clarify -- I will clarify the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I referred to the bottom left corner, where we can see the name of Dr. Hasandic.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You're welcome, Your Honour. Thank you, Ms. Usher. You can take this exhibit and I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In late June of 1992, what was the operation, the large operation carried out in Posavina region?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: In June of 1992, the Army of Republika Srpska carried out a military operation trying to break through the corridor in Posavina region.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you know the reasons behind that military operation, even though you are not a military expert?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: The reason for that was total encirclement of all Krajina Serbs, of Bosnian Krajina, Western Slavonia and Croatian Krajina, and the inability to bring in equipment and materiel. So all of that caused the Army of Republika Srpska to try to carry out this break-through and open up the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Military administration was introduced in Odzak at that time. Do you know something about that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: When the Army of Republika Srpska entered the municipality of Odzak, there was nobody there. And then General Talic issued an order introducing military administration, a military rule in the territory of that municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What was the goal of that military administration?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The Serb refugees from Odzak, those who were staying in Samac at the time, did they go back to their hearths?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Mostly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: How was their return and their normal life in Odzak made possible? How was the electricity provided to them and all the things?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: The state companies that had branch offices in the territory of Odzak before transferred their workers there and opened up the vital systems, electric power supply, water supply, telephone lines, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did military authorities request the Crisis Staff of Samac and other surrounding municipalities to nominate candidates or representatives for the council that dealt with civilian matters in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Military authorities in Odzak asked the surrounding municipalities to send everyone who wasn't engaged sufficiently in neighbouring municipalities to the municipality of Odzak providing that they were from that municipality originally.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So which civilians from the municipality of Samac were nominated to give their contribution to the establishment of civilian government in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: All of those who, by the opinion of the Ministry of Defence, were believed not to have been sufficiently engaged in Samac municipality. They were sent there pursuant to a document of the Ministry of Defence. Savo Popovic was considered surplus in the Crisis Staff, and all other companies also sent some of their personnel there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you know perhaps who was commander of that military administration?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: The first commander of military administration was General Novica Simic, who at the time was colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: How long did he remain in that post?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't know that exactly, but I think that there was a change in commanders every two months.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you personally go to Odzak? Did you have any contacts with the officials from the military administration?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Very seldom. Only upon being invited to go there, because I wasn't able to go there without a pass issued by them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, may I seek further clarification. And I suggest it will help everyone concerned. The witness said that people -- civilians who were sent from Samac were those who in the opinion of the Ministry of Defence were believed not to have been sufficiently engaged in Samac municipality. The way that's translated into English, I just don't understand what that means. "Sufficiently engaged," engaged in what? And secondly, the witness started to tell us of some of the civilians who were sent there. He mentioned Savo Popovic. You may care to know if any other civilians were also sent to -- or any other Samac -- Bosanski Samac people were also sent to Odzak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think that touches on one of the crucial issues in the indictment; that should be for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: If we could have a break now, Your Honour. It's 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. We shall resume our proceedings at 11.30 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic, you're continuing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Simic, before we continue, let us go back to a topic that has to do with what we discussed in the morning. Do you know something about whether in May or June exchanges were organised between the Serb and the Croat side?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I think that during that time there was just one exchange organised, and at that it was organised by the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you know roughly how many people were exchanged on that occasion, on the Serb side and on the Croat side?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I think it was 100 for 100.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. And just one more question regarding that: What was the role of the security organs, both civilian and military, in that exchange process? Specifically, did the civilian and military security organs have to issue a prior consent for this to go on?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Without the approval of all security services, the exchanges could not take place. And by this, I refer both to civilian and military organs and all three warring sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We mentioned the presence of a number of volunteers from Serbia who were in Stevan Todorovic's circle. What was your experience in context with these people? Did you have any problems with them, and did other people, your colleagues from the Crisis Staff, have any problems in dealing with them? What was your viewpoint regarding this?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: A part of them -- or rather, all of them were under the command of the then-Yugoslav People's Army. A part of them after the war operations would come into town and cause problems there. They would usually be drunk and cause trouble to anyone they would meet. Some of them --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Yes. Page 34 and line 8, the accused is speaking about Stevan Todorovic's circle. Could you give me an explanation on what is meant by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You heard His Honour Lindholm. Could you please explain what was the relationship between Stevan Todorovic and these people.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Stevan Todorovic was not a serious person. Nobody considered him as such. And in order to raise the level of his own importance and in wartime also the level of his authority, he tried to surround himself with certain individuals and abuse them at the same time, and these people were seen in Stevan Todorovic's company on various occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you personally have any problems with these people and with Stevan Todorovic?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I have had problems with Stevan Todorovic from 1990 to this day, and almost all other members of the Crisis Staff were harassed by Stevan Todorovic and by some of these other people, volunteers. And here I have Milos Bogdanovic in mind, first and foremost, about whom Stevan Todorovic invented a story that he sold a publicly owned camera, and later on this man went to the front line and got killed there. Later on, he harassed Mirko Ivanovic, a member of the executive council, who didn't want to come back from Serbia any more. He also harassed Fadil Topcagic and invented all kinds of stories about this man and mostly laughed at every move he made. He also harassed Miroslav Tadic. The volunteers on several occasions stirred up trouble in his coffee-shop many times and several times forced him to perform some improper acts, which he had to do in their presence, and so on. Stevan Todorovic had awfully bad relations with me, starting in 1990, and this always used to culminate in fierce arguments.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can you give us the names of some of those volunteers that you were in conflict with or who badgered you?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: The largest number of those volunteers and probably the most delinquent psychopathological personality was Lugar, who I think not a day would pass without causing some incident, wherever he might happen to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you try to do something in this regard to stop such incidents, that is, the perpetrators of such incidents?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: With Stevan Todorovic, it was almost impossible to achieve. And the brigade commander, that is, the brigade command was about 40 kilometres away. And when the brigade engaged them on the front and in combat operations, then peace reigned in the municipality and in the town itself. But the chaos would start after their return from the front and when they would count their fatalities, their dead and their wounded, and that is when the trouble started. It was only -- the strengthening of the state and the strengthening of the Army of Republika Srpska is the thing to do, and especially when General Talic arrived in the area, who across the area covered by the 1st Krajina Corps arrested all the groups and all the individuals who were not under the command of the Army of Republika Srpska. So he arrested the group in Prnjavor, in Doboj, in Modrica, in Samac, in Srpsko Orasje, in Brcko, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Another episode in -- we've heard a number of testimonies --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Which time period are you now talking?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You've heard the question of His Honour Judge Lindholm. What period are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about April, May, June. So end of April, May, and June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Which year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In this case, we heard several testimonies about white armbands that allegedly were worn by members of non-Serb ethnicity in Samac. Were you aware of this phenomenon? I'm talk about mid-April 1992 onward.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Apart from the soldiers, I didn't see anyone else wear such ribbons. I never heard anyone request that such ribbons be worn. I did not see any order or heard an order requesting that such ribbons be worn, and I can say under full responsibility that they are not ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Were there any such announcements, that is, orders, on the radio that non-Serbs in Samac were to wear such white ribbons or armbands?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: There was no such announcement on the radio to wear them, but I have to add that radio did not work; primarily because there was no electricity, and secondly because the aerial system had burnt down on the 17th of April, when the elementary school also burnt down. And before that, it was only a 300-watt radio station, so it could barely cover the centre of the town, that is, the kind of power that people have in their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that there is some inconsistency here in the transcript. It's page 34, line -- I'm looking at the laptop, actually. Line 25. The witness says, "And I can say under full responsibility that they are not ours." Actually, this is not what he said. It doesn't have any sense, I mean, speaking about ours, our white ribbons or something like that. He was talking about not wearing any white ribbons. And that was the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe -- Mr. Pantelic, please clarify that with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I will just try to find on my machine. 34, line 25 -- 37? Uh-huh. I can see your response, "And I can say under full responsibility that they are not ours."

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Uh-huh. Very well. Right, Dr. Simic, let's clear this up. In that answer you said that apart from the soldiers, you didn't see anyone else wearing those ribbons or armbands, that you didn't know -- that you were sure that nobody requested anybody to wear it and that you claim under full responsibility that -- what?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: These were not worn by any civilians that I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: This answer requires a supplementary question. Does that mean that you never saw a civilian wearing white armbands?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I did not see a single civilian wearing these white ribbons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And did the Crisis Staff ever discuss that possibility at all, to order civilians to wear those white ribbons?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff never discussed that possibility, nor is there -- nor was there any reason for anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And tell us, you mentioned that the soldiers wore those white armbands. Where? On which part of their uniform did they wear them? What did they look like, and do you know why did they wear them?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: The soldiers wore them so that -- as a sign of identification on the front. At times they were yellow, at times they were red, and at times they were white. And usually they would have them on their shoulders, because all three sides had similar uniforms and on the front it was very difficult to tell one soldier from the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In July or in late July you were wounded and you were in a hospital in Brcko and then the clinical setting in Belgrade. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: For the benefit of my learned friend, it's R15/1, 2, 3, and 4. This is a medical documentation that we have been -- that we have provided to you. I would like to tender it in evidence, the medical documentations with regard to the episode that we just want to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I have no objections, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. Can we have the numbers, pleas.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Dr. Simic, look at this documentation. And since you are a doctor, just a few words about what this is about.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, it will be D60/1 and D60/1 ter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: This is a bullet wound in the upper right leg, a bullet which went through the leg, with the obliteration of the blood vessels.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You were treated in the medical centre in Samac first, then in Brcko, and finally you were admitted into the clinical centre in Belgrade. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And when were you wounded?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Why, on the 23rd, 23rd of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Which year?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And what were the circumstances of your wounding?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: The circumstances were those of the self-inflicted wound. Inadvertently, I wounded myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So that is -- I mean, so that it was an accident. It just happened by accident?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: How did it happen? What did you have -- what was the weapon that wounded you and what happened to the weapon? Did it fall, or when it fired by itself, what happened?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I was cleaning my pistol, and that is when it fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And how long did your rehabilitation last altogether? I don't mean only the period in the hospital, but also the post-operative one.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, it was three or four months, except that my condition did not improve for a long time, that is, until the beginning of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Were the major blood vessels in your leg injured?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I would like to tender these exhibits into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: I have a question here. When counsel asked how did it happen, and so on, the answer was, "I was cleaning my pistol and that is when it fired." I am an old officer in the Finnish army, and pistols don't fire when you're cleaning them. So if you could clarify this situation for us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You heard His Honour Judge Lindholm's question. Will you give us some more details about this.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, it is an outdated model of a TT pistol, Zastava pistol, and it's bad properties that it fires off when it drops. And so I was cleaning, and it fell, and so it went off, and that is how my leg was wounded. These old Zastava pistols, not all Zastava pistols are like that, but this was an older model of Zastava TT pistol. And when it fell -- when they fall, they simply go off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me. I just have one question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: On the same issue. In the English translation of the case history and medical findings, the current illness of yourself in that case, Dr. Simic, is listed as "war injury," not "self-inflicted injury." Presumably the doctor wrote down what the doctor was told when you presented your case, so I find this a little strange. I'm looking at page 3 of the English translation, and at the bottom right-hand corner it's signed by Dr. Sego.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We shall clarify that. Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So as far as I understood, you could not take the pistol apart, cleaning its parts. You were cleaning the outside of the pistol, and it fell and went off.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I was cleaning it whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Does that satisfy your inquiry, Your Honour, this -- these details?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. But that was the response to Judge Lindholm's question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. And now I clarify that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: My question was totally different.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now tell me, since your hospital documents say that it was a war injury and that you had arrived from the war-affected area, that is, in Brcko, would you please explain to us the mechanism. How are these reports typed and on the basis of what information? Do they include all the details and in view of the circumstances and all that? Can you give us some more details? Because you're a doctor, after all.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I do not know why it says "war injury," but I had arrived with all the other wounded from Brcko during the war. Brcko was the centre hospital where all the wounded were brought from the front, and then forwarded -- sent down to Belgrade, where the teams on duty would admit them and then operate on them and look after them. There was no reason for the word "war" to be put there because it was an injury that I had inflicted on myself inadvertently. True, in the war-affected area, but I had injured myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So in that period afterwards you underwent certain rehabilitation. Tell me, in the month of August 1992, were you in Odzak in a house with a swimming pool where some of the members of the Samac population were doing their work obligations inter alia a female witness who testified before this Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I was not at any swimming pool in Odzak, nor do I know where this is, nor do I know of its existence at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In September 1992 and upon the request of then-Colonel Simic, who was military commander, did you discuss at the Crisis Staff the arrival of volunteers from Serbia for the second time in that zone?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I did not attend such a meeting of the Crisis Staff. Actually, of the War Presidency. At that time, there was no Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of some letter of the War Presidency that was addressed to this group of volunteers so that they would have a basis for coming and joining the military operations taking place there at the time?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I cannot recall that we wrote any letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge in respect of these volunteers reappearing in the area in the autumn of 1992?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We are going to move on to November 1992. During the proceedings, the Prosecutor exhibited the letter of 13 signatories, as it is called here. Tell me briefly, what circumstances were involved regarding the writing of this letter, then relations between the military structures and civilian authorities, and the possible resolution of these problems?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat this question for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of this letter that indicates certain omissions in the work of the civilian authorities that was signed by 13 members of the military, that is to say, officers and soldiers?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. But we called that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What do you know about this information and generally speaking about the circumstances that are relevant to the creation of that information?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: The executive board said that they had obtained a document that is confidential, secret, at the brigade command in Pelagicevo, on the territory of the municipality of Pelagicevo, 40 kilometres away. This had to do with the problems in the municipality of Samac as well. The information had both positive and negative parts. That was our assessment then. And the executive board proposed that the municipal parliament be convened and that this information be presented before the municipal parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what were the positive and what were the negative assessments regarding this information, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: The positive ones were that crime was being pointed out, and there was crime, both in the area of the military and among the people themselves. And this also indicated some omissions on the part of the civilian authorities that indeed did take place. As for the negative, the first document envisaged a struggle for power -- rather, the imposing of military rule. Secondly, the territory of the municipality of Pelagicevo, the municipality of Srpsko Orasje, the municipality of Samac, and the municipality of Odzak were not clearly spelled out. It was written in general terms and the problems varied from one municipality to the other. We thought that the executive board of the Municipal Assembly of Samac and the command of the brigade should overcome this problem through talks between themselves, which indeed they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone for Mr. Pantelic.
